steps.label: A conditional spectrum · 1/6
steps.speakerNotes: KP15's two results are only two of the many convergence theories the source lists, which sorts the others into three directions. First, activations: quadratic, ReLU, Leaky ReLU.

steps.label: A conditional spectrum · 1/6 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Second, architectures: residual connections and non-i.i.d. data streams.

steps.label: A conditional spectrum · 1/6 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Third, geometry and bounds: characterizing critical points and the implicit bias of cross-entropy.

steps.label: A conditional spectrum · 1/6 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: geometry and bounds characterizing critical points, the implicit bias of cross-entropy

steps.label: A conditional spectrum · 1/6 (4)
steps.speakerNotes: Their common form is KP15's: if the assumptions hold, the training loss is small.

steps.label: A conditional spectrum · 1/6 (5)
steps.speakerNotes: Not that the test loss is small. Reading any such result, first ask: does my problem meet its assumptions, and is it the training loss that is guaranteed or something else?

steps.label: The toolchain · 2/6
steps.speakerNotes: The whole chapter is a chain of questions, each unit answering one.

steps.label: The toolchain · 2/6 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: The first rows: what training is, how far per step, how the gradient is computed, KP01 to KP06.

steps.label: The toolchain · 2/6 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Then: can we afford it and can the step adapt per coordinate, KP07 to KP11.

steps.label: The toolchain · 2/6 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Finally: is one point's loss enough, why non-convex still trains, and after training, KP12 to KP16. Every tool on the chain has a cost and conditions; none answers every question.

steps.label: Answered and open · 3/6
steps.speakerNotes: Four things are answered: gradients can be computed cheaply; GD and SGD behavior is analyzable under clear conditions; adaptive steps and the worst neighborhood loss are derived designs; under over-parameterization and similar conditions the training loss provably goes to any small value.

steps.label: Answered and open · 3/6 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Three remain open: why it generalizes, since the theorem does not say which solution is reached; whether flatness causes generalization, since curvature depends on parameterization; how to compare optimizers, which needs controlled experiments.

steps.label: Answered and open · 3/6 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: After training we still ask: how does it do on unseen data?

steps.label: Answered and open · 3/6 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: after training we still ask: how does it do on unseen data? this chapter's tools make training work; “why it generalizes” goes to the next

steps.label: Three sets · 4/6
steps.speakerNotes: Each of the three sets has a job. The training set tunes the parameters and answers whether the training objective fell.

steps.label: Three sets · 4/6 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: The validation set chooses models and hyperparameters and answers who is better in a controlled comparison.

steps.label: Three sets · 4/6 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: The test set is touched once at the end and answers how it performs on untouched data.

steps.label: Three sets · 4/6 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Choosing a model by training loss picks the one that memorizes best.

steps.label: Three sets · 4/6 (4)
steps.speakerNotes: choosing by training loss picks the model that memorizes best the three sets are disjoint

steps.label: The polynomial example · 5/6
steps.speakerNotes: A recomputable example: the true curve is sine of 3x with label noise std 0.2, so the best test error is 0.04. Fit polynomials of different degrees by least squares.

steps.label: The polynomial example · 5/6 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Degree 3: training 0.026, validation 0.0533, test 0.0571, close to the noise floor.

steps.label: The polynomial example · 5/6 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Degree 14, parameters equal to the number of samples: training 0, validation 1072, test 164.76, the worst.

steps.label: The polynomial example · 5/6 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Degree 24, more parameters than data: training 0, validation 0.5197, test 0.8247, far better than degree 14 but still worse than degree 3.

steps.label: The polynomial example · 5/6 (4)
steps.speakerNotes: Choosing by training loss picks degree 14 with test 164.76.

steps.label: The polynomial example · 5/6 (5)
steps.speakerNotes: Choosing by validation loss picks degree 3 with test 0.0571. The validation number is slightly optimistic, so report on the untouched test set.

steps.label: Myths and next question · 6/6
steps.speakerNotes: Finally, the common myths and the question left for the next unit.

steps.speakerNotes: “a convergence theorem proves the model predicts well”. it guarantees training loss; test performance needs validation and test evidence

steps.label: Myths and next question · 6/6 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: “this chapter's best tool is Adam plus SAM”. each tool answers a different question with conditions: no universal best

steps.label: Myths and next question · 6/6 (4)
steps.speakerNotes: However low the training loss, a model may just memorize. How do we control complexity and avoid overfitting?
